political demands.

pressed fears that West Berlin

gone too far in their direct

policy of not recognizing the
Communist Berlin government.

occupation.

Public outrage at the ruinous dam
age to the Potomac River valley above
Washington already has forced the Army
Engineers to beat prudent retreat from
one high-level dam propoSal-at River
Bend, Md. 1t is apparent now that their
substitute dam at Seneca, few miles
upriver, Is no more acceptable. For this
impoundment would spare only limited
area from its massive inundation. It's
waters still would destroy historic scenic
and recreational resources, creep over
private and public property on both
sides of the river, and back up the
Potomac nearly to Harper's Ferry.


This lamentable destruction could
be defended If there were no other way
to solve the most urgent Potomac River
problem-an adequate supply of water
for the Nations Capital. But that is not
the case. Many experts are convinced
that series of more modest impound-
ments on the Potomac and its tribu-
tarieS above Harper'S Ferry, coupled
with the normal flow Of the river, would
suffice for long, long time-and leave
the natural character of the main stem
Of the river intact.


The authors of the Seneca plan do
not contend that it Is justified by water
supply needs alone. They argue that the
waters Of this dam also are needed for
pollution control, and that its reservoir
would create new and more valuable
recreational resources. But on these
points, too, the evidence does not sup
port the claims.


Consider pollution. The plan is that
during periods Of low river flow, large
quantities Of water could be released to
surge down the river bed and flush the
pollution away. Certainly the day is not
far off when research and technology
will produce better method than this.
Indeed, experts even today differ as to
the effectiveness of the flushing" tech
nique. At the public hearing last week,
for example, David V. Aud, the Districts
sanitary engineering director, expressed
uncertainty about its value, and urged
that attention be paid first to "other
0ollution-con alternatives" This is
sound advice.


The Engineers are most vulner-
able, however, in their claims for
the recreational values which would
accrue to the public from the big dams.
For these values, whatever they may be,
would require the destruction Of the
infinitely greater natural values Of the
Potomac Valley. Surely the Army En-
gineerS can develop a plan which will
offer the people of the Potomac Basin
a better choice than that.

week because Of rising construc-

ing Contractors called on all
members to revoke the work
suspension order in view of the
rioting.

hour traffic moving through the
Piazza Venezia area were caught
unawares as the clash broke
out.

and the famous square was left
Uttered with damaged auto


actor scooters and
and shattered glass. Fighting
spread into side streets.

repercussions in parliament.

vention by the cabinet of

There can be no reasonable doubt
about the urgent need for the $29.9-
million school bond issue to be placed
before Fairfax voters at the county ref
erendum tomorrow. Unexpectedly high
enrollmentS during the last few years
have completely exhausted the school
construction funds provided by bonds
in 1860. And the outlook now facing
the county is that approximately 1000
additional children win enter public
schools during each Of the next three
years.


Failure of the bond issue could lead
to only two alternatives. Either school
facilities would become utterly made
quate, resulting in double shifts and
makeShift quarters, or the necessary
funds for new school construction
would have to come from current op-
Grating revenues - requiring, in turn,
pyramiding increases in the county
tax rate. Under the bond plan, costs of
the proposed 10 new elementary schools,
three new intermediate schools and
three new high schools would be retired
over a number Of years, in large part by
future residents of the county.


These are the pertinent facts which
have generated near-unanimous support
for the bond issue from Fairfax officials
and from the organized civic, business
and professional groups which have
studied the problem. The danger is,
however, that this widespread indorse-
ment may create false sense of secur-
ity-an atmosphere Of apathy which, if
enough voters stay away from the polls,
could allow determined minority to
scuttle the program. Every registered
Fairfax voter should turn out to assure
construction Of these vitality needed
new buildings.

Just 80 years ago a tide of ra-

der.

ris, editor of the Salisbury Times,
